title: The child's top
hookLine: like an old man keeping a child's toy, comfort others without being swept away (Meditations 5.36)

lines: AN OLD MAN AND A TOP.
cards: A four-year-old drops an ice cream cone on the sidewalk. The wail is total. The world has ended.
Two grown-ups are standing there. One says, it's only ice cream, stop crying. The other kneels down, says, oh no, your cone, and holds the child until the storm passes.

Neither of them thinks the cone was a tragedy. Only one of them was any comfort. Near the end of book five, Marcus Aurelius has a picture for the second grown-up: an old man and a child's spinning top.

teach.b: Marcus believes most of what people grieve over isn't truly harmful: money, a post, a reputation. Only acting badly harms the self. That could make a Stoic cold.
Someone loses their job, and the Stoic says, that's an indifferent, you're fine.

teach.h: THE OLD MAN AND THE TOP.
teach.b: Marcus doesn't want that. In book five, entry thirty-six, he says: don't be carried away by how things look.
Help people as far as you can and as each case deserves, even when what they've lost is one of those indifferent things. But don't imagine the loss is a real harm to them; that's a bad habit of mind.
Then the picture: be like the old man who, when he was leaving, asked for his foster child's top back, remembering all along that it was a top. He takes the toy seriously because the child does.
He just doesn't forget what it is.
An honest note: the Greek here is compressed, and the end of this section is partly damaged in the manuscripts.
Translators fill the gaps in different ways, and scholars still argue about exactly what the old man is doing.
The core is clear enough: kindness on the outside, clarity on the inside. The old man never lies to the child, and he doesn't lecture.
He meets the child where the child is, and keeps his own head. That's a skill most of us need at a hospital bedside, a breakup, a lost game. Be warm with the sorrow.
Stay clear about the size of things, privately.

how: People who practice Stoic ethics often describe comforting others warmly while keeping their own judgment about what is truly harmful, rather than either lecturing or catching the panic.

o: the Stoic who comforted warmly but saw losses clearly
the emperor who taught that every loss is a real harm
the Stoic who told grieving people to stop crying

games.q: the child's top — tap the pairs.
p: asks back the top, knowing it's a top

s: Marcus says not to help people whose losses are only 'indifferent'
he says help them as far as you can, just don't believe the loss truly harms them.
the end of Meditations 5.36 is damaged and hard to translate
translators fill the gaps differently, and scholars still argue about the old man.
the old man lies to the child about the top's value
he plays along kindly, but never forgets it's a top.

games.q: a friend is crushed that a small plan fell through. you think it doesn't matter much. what do you do?
o: comfort them warmly, and keep your own sense of its size.
get as upset as they are.
games.why: Marcus's old man takes the top seriously for the child's sake while remembering it's a top: warm outside, clear inside.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is upset right now about something you think is small, a canceled trip, a lost game, a broken phone, and notice the urge to fix it with a fact.
Set the fact down, and picture saying, oh no, that's hard, and meaning it. Notice that you can still see the size of the thing: both at once.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, whose old man treats a toy seriously because the child does, without forgetting that it's only a toy. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a spinning top (also a spiral shell), the toy in Meditations 5.36.

carryVoice: Your line: honest comfort. Warm with the sorrow, clear about the size. Gently, until tomorrow.
